https://local12.com/news/local/woman-sen.text: GALLATIN COUNTY, Ky. (WKRC) - A woman was sentenced to 14 years in prison Friday for stabbing a man multiple times in Gallatin County last year. Michelle Anderson pleaded guilty in June in connection with the March 2025 stabbing at an apartment on Third Street in Warsaw. The victim was stabbed multiple times and flown to a hospital by medical helicopter. Anderson received her 14-year prison sentence Friday.

https://english.news.cn/europe/20261026/.text: NATO brigade launches major exercise in eastern Latvia RIGA, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The NATO Multinational Brigade in Latvia is staging its largest force deployment exercise from Oct. 26 to 28, the Latvian Defense Ministry has announced. Around 3,000 troops and 1,000 pieces of military equipment will participate in the Resolute Reforger 2026 drills in eastern Latvia. During the exercise, brigade units are set to perform force deployment, supply, command and communication tasks, as well as enhance interoperability with the Latvian army. The exercise aims to test the brigade's ability to move, supply and coordinate units over long distances. Colonel David Brassard, commander of the NATO Multinational Brigade, said the exercise would provide an opportunity for the brigade to demonstrate its ability to deploy combat-ready forces over long distances, sustain them in the field, and maintain effective command, control and communications throughout the exercise. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily

https://www.sciencealert.com/seeing-your.text: Seeing Your Pain Through an Evolutionary Lens May Ease Depression, Early Trial Finds Health 01 November 2026 By Esra Öz (Joshua Eghelshi/Pexels) After a relationship ends, loneliness can come with questions. Why does it still hurt? Why can't I move on? For someone experiencing depressive symptoms, searching for an answer can become another way to blame themselves. Scientists in Romania examined a therapy that aims to reduce this self-blame by exploring how the pain of separation relates to needs for closeness and security shaped throughout human evolution. The researchers adapted the therapy into two intensive days of group treatment. In a preliminary trial involving 61 adults with depressive symptoms, those assigned to the program showed substantially greater improvement one week later than people on a waiting list. The program builds on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which addresses connections between thoughts, feelings, and behavior. After a breakup, someone who sees themselves as worthless might withdraw from others, deepening their loneliness. CBT can help people recognize and change such patterns. The approach tested here, called cognitive evolutionary therapy , also considers how difficulties involving belonging, close relationships, and safety connect with needs important to our ancestors. "The perspective of evolutionary therapy adds another level to the usual cognitive-behavioral approach," Mihai Dobrovolschi, a clinical psychologist and researcher at the University of Bucharest, told ScienceAlert. Dobrovolschi offered losing a partner as an example. Understanding how consequential that loss could have been for our ancestors might help someone respond to their distress with less self-criticism, he explained. "It changes 'What's wrong with me?' to 'What important problem am I reacting to, and what can I do about it?'" Dobrovolschi said. To evaluate the program, the team randomly assigned 31 adults to therapy and 30 to a waiting list. Before sessions, participants completed questionnaires identifying difficulties across their lives. The researchers suggest this preparation could allow therapeutic work to begin sooner. Sessions took place in Bucharest, in groups of five to seven, across two consecutive 8-hour days. Although treatment occupied only two days, it involved 16 hours of therapy, roughly the contact time of a standard 12- to 16-session course of individual CBT. How the two-day group therapy worked: participants completed questionnaires, then attended 16 hours of therapy over two days in groups of five to seven. Researchers assessed their symptoms at one week and at three months later. (Dobrovolschi et al., BMC Psychology , 2026) The therapist worked individually with participants in front of the group, followed by structured feedback and discussion. No between-session homework was assigned. The researchers suggest that discussing shared struggles might help participants feel less alone, although they haven't tested these explanations for improvement. The trial joins research into brief interventions for depressive symptoms , with this program concentrating therapist support and group work into two days. Researchers assessed symptoms before treatment, one week afterward, and at three months. Their depression questionnaire covered experiences such as hopelessness and difficulty enjoying things, with higher scores indicating more severe symptoms. At one week, the adjusted difference between groups was about 7.5 points in favor of therapy on the 0-to-42 scale, a large statistical effect. Anxiety and life satisfaction also improved. Three months later, however, the estimated depression-score advantage had shrunk to about 3.1 points and was no longer statistically significant. "With a relatively small sample, we simply cannot say with confidence whether a meaningful effect persisted," Dobrovolschi said. The initial benefit may have weakened. Dobrovolschi also noted that waiting-list participants improved over those months. Follow-up sessions might help maintain gains, but the trial did not test them. Six people assigned to therapy never attended, leaving 25 who received it. Seven waiting-list participants were lost before the three-month assessment. Participants were mostly women. One therapist delivered all treatment, recruited participants, and assigned them to groups, so he knew beforehand who would receive therapy. Co-author Cezar Giosan developed the therapy and its manual. The researchers acknowledged that developers may unintentionally influence results in their own trials and called for independent replication. Formal depression diagnoses were not required, and outcomes relied on self-report, so the findings can't establish recovery from a diagnosed disorder. A waiting-list comparison cannot show the program works better than existing therapies or separate evolutionary explanations from attention, expectations, and group support. A larger trial comparing the program with standard group cognitive behavioral therapy could clarify its contribution. Running it in other cities with different therapists, adding clinician assessments, and following participants for longer would help show whether results hold and gains endure. "If that finding can be replicated under more stringent conditions and shown to last, the brevity of the intervention could become clinically and practically important," Dobrovolschi said. The research has been published in BMC Psychology . This article was fact-checked by Rachel Garner and edited by Rebecca Dyer . While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human.
